steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on federated learning via lattice joint source-channel coding. Review quantization and over-the-air approaches to FL and their limitations, motivate blind transmission, and present our scheme and its key contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- FL and its communication issues; lattice-based quantization for FL
- Over-the-air FL and its assumptions (analog modulation, CSIT, power control, synchronization)
- One-bit / BPSK over-the-air FL
- Blind transmission and prior blind over-the-air FL
- Our proposal: lattice joint source-channel coding
- Contributions: compute-update scheme, transmitter-receiver architecture, system insights

  - lower cost/resources but high latency, performance gap vs non-quantized (cite)
  - channel estimation and power control issues remain
- Blind transmission
  - most wireless systems: constant power, blind, no channel adjustment
  - no CSIT/power control; average energy maintained; dynamic range not enlarged -> simpler, cheaper hardware
  - transmitter-side channel adjustment suffers from estimation errors, unpredictable gains (cite)
  - blind over-the-air FL strategy (cite): receiver equalization, needs many antennas; fading impact diminishes as antenna count grows without bound
  - blind over-the-air FL without compensating fading (cite)

  - blind: no prior knowledge or CSIT

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
With the rise of advanced wireless edge devices, federated learning (FL) deals with challenges like data privacy, latency, and bandwidth by letting machine learning processing happen locally, so the data stays on the device. In wireless settings that are dense with IoT devices and have network constraints, FL has communication problems. FL methods that use orthogonal multiple access transmission avoid interference, but they cause latency and need more resources. To deal with these challenges, prior works have used a source coding scheme based on lattice codes to quantize the model parameters in FL. One of them also considers privacy enhancement. This lattice-based quantization is based on the principles of subtractive dithered lattice quantization, which is grounded in information-theoretic arguments. One of these methods gives a more precise finite-bit representation for FL than traditional scalar quantization methods. In a sense, it uses functional quantization.

Another strategy is over-the-air computation, which makes use of the interference from edge devices transmitting at the same time. Over-the-air FL is built on this and handles FL aggregation in the presence of interference, so it is more efficient, uses fewer resources, and is faster than FL with orthogonal transmission. But previous research on over-the-air FL assumed analog modulation, where the transmitter can shape the carrier waveform freely by choosing any real number I/Q coefficients. This may not be possible for existing wireless devices, because they have digital modulation chips that may not support arbitrary modulation schemes. Also, past work follows a power control approach and needs perfect channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT) for all devices, to set their transmission powers and counteract wireless channel effects during aggregation. In this approach there are physical constraints on both the instantaneous and the average transmission power. So a device with poor channel conditions may either not be able to take part in the learning process or have to use very high power. Past work also needs perfect synchronization among the transmitters. These requirements lead to a large overhead for channel estimation training and feedback before any transmission, which increases delays and reduces spectral efficiency.

The special case of over-the-air FL with BPSK modulation has also been studied. One-bit quantization reduces the implementation cost and the resource requirements a lot, but it can cause high latency and a performance gap compared to the non-quantized case. Also, the other challenges about channel estimation and power control are still there.

  - blind over-the-air FL without compensating fading (cite)
- Our proposal
  - joint source-channel coding; transmission and aggregation strategies with lattice codes, adjustable quantization levels
  - resilience against noise and interference; works with limited number of server antennas
  - blind: no prior knowledge or CSIT
  - inspired by nested lattice coding based modulation in compute-and-forward relaying (cite)
- Contributions
  - Compute-Update Scheme: FedCPU; lattice quantization with normalization and dithering; decode one integer combination as lattice point; additive structure of aggregation; Voronoi region protects against decoding error, absent in analog schemes (cite); adjustable aggregation vs fixed predefined weights (equal or local dataset size) from the seminal FL paper (cite), used throughout over-the-air FL (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
With the rise of advanced wireless edge devices, federated learning (FL) deals with challenges like data privacy, latency, and bandwidth by letting machine learning processing happen locally, so the data stays on the device. In wireless settings that are dense with IoT devices and have network constraints, FL has communication problems. FL methods that use orthogonal multiple access transmission avoid interference, but they cause latency and need more resources. To deal with these challenges, prior works have used a source coding scheme based on lattice codes to quantize the model parameters in FL. One of them also considers privacy enhancement. This lattice-based quantization is based on the principles of subtractive dithered lattice quantization, which is grounded in information-theoretic arguments. One of these methods gives a more precise finite-bit representation for FL than traditional scalar quantization methods. In a sense, it uses functional quantization.

Another strategy is over-the-air computation, which makes use of the interference from edge devices transmitting at the same time. Over-the-air FL is built on this and handles FL aggregation in the presence of interference, so it is more efficient, uses fewer resources, and is faster than FL with orthogonal transmission. But previous research on over-the-air FL assumed analog modulation, where the transmitter can shape the carrier waveform freely by choosing any real number I/Q coefficients. This may not be possible for existing wireless devices, because they have digital modulation chips that may not support arbitrary modulation schemes. Also, past work follows a power control approach and needs perfect channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT) for all devices, to set their transmission powers and counteract wireless channel effects during aggregation. In this approach there are physical constraints on both the instantaneous and the average transmission power. So a device with poor channel conditions may either not be able to take part in the learning process or have to use very high power. Past work also needs perfect synchronization among the transmitters. These requirements lead to a large overhead for channel estimation training and feedback before any transmission, which increases delays and reduces spectral efficiency.

The special case of over-the-air FL with BPSK modulation has also been studied. One-bit quantization reduces the implementation cost and the resource requirements a lot, but it can cause high latency and a performance gap compared to the non-quantized case. Also, the other challenges about channel estimation and power control are still there.

Most wireless systems use constant power for blind transmission and do not adjust directly for the channel. Besides not needing CSIT and power control, this approach has several advantages. First, it keeps the average energy for signal transmission the same no matter how the channel varies. Also, it stops the dynamic range of the transmitted signal from getting larger, which makes hardware implementation much simpler and cheaper. Finally, approaches that adjust for the channel at the transmitter can have channel estimation errors, so the values get multiplied by unpredictable gains when they are received. Because of this, one work proposes a blind over-the-air FL strategy. But this method suggests a particular receiver equalization and so it needs a large number of receiver antennas, and the impact of wireless fading gets smaller as the antenna count grows without bound. Other works look at blind over-the-air FL that does not compensate for the bad effects of fading.

In this work we propose a joint source-channel coding scheme with new transmission and aggregation strategies that use lattice codes with adjustable quantization levels. We develop a new coding base, and our aim is to make over-the-air FL more resilient against noise and interference, so that the desired learning outcomes are achieved. In particular this gives effective performance in hard channel conditions, even with a limited number of antennas at the server. Our approach is blind and does not rely on any prior knowledge or CSIT. It is inspired by past research which shows the advantages of nested lattice coding based modulation in compute-and-forward relaying as a channel coding scheme, which improves bit-rate throughput at relays. The key contributions are the following.

Compute-Update Scheme: We give an end-to-end framework for transmitting real-valued model parameters in FL, which we call compute-update FL— FedCPU. At the transmitter, we develop lattice codes to quantize the model parameters. The quantization is based on normalization and dithering. At the server, we decode one integer combination of the transmitted quantized model parameters as a lattice point, and after processing this gives a new form of aggregation. We use integer combinations because the aggregation of model parameters in FL has an additive structure. Also, the lattice Voronoi region over the decoded integer combination protects against the decoding error that comes from interference and noise. Analog modulation schemes do not have this protection, since their transmitted values are continuous. In addition, the adjustable aggregation method we propose is a big change from the usual practice in FL of using fixed, predefined weights, which are either equal or based on the size of the local datasets. This usual approach was recommended for ideal, error-free communication in the seminal FL paper, and it has been used consistently in over-the-air FL research. This is the case even though over-the-air FL deals with imperfect communication, with interference and noise. In response, our method tailors the aggregation weights to the wide range of decoding errors of each integer combination in our model.

Transmitter-Receiver Architecture: To do the aggregation, we propose a two-layer receiver architecture at the server that uses both the real and imaginary parts of the signal. The first layer has an equalization vector, which is then optimized to minimize the decoding error. In the second layer, a normalizing factor is introduced and optimized to minimize the quantization error.

System Insights: Our experiments show that FedCPU is effective in handling the lack of CSIT and having only a limited number of antennas at the server. Shrinking the lattice Voronoi regions shows a balance between more decoding error and less quantization error. FedCPU has much better learning accuracy than other over-the-air schemes, because of its distinctive aggregation technique and finely-tuned receiver design. The learning results closely follow what is expected with ideal, error-free orthogonal transmission.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Given the rise of advanced wireless edge devices, federated learning (FL) addresses challenges such as data privacy, latency, and bandwidth by enabling local machine learning processing, so that data remains on-device [1]. In IoT-dense wireless settings with network constraints, FL faces communication issues. FL methods using orthogonal multiple access transmission prevent interference, but they result in latency and require more resources [2]. To address these challenges, a source coding scheme based on lattice codes has been used in [3,4] to quantize model parameters in FL, and [4] also considers privacy enhancement. This lattice-based quantization builds on the principles of subtractive dithered lattice quantization [5], which is grounded in information-theoretic arguments. The method in [3] offers a more precise finite-bit representation for FL than traditional scalar quantization methods; in a sense, it uses functional quantization [6].

Leveraging the interference from simultaneous edge device transmissions, over-the-air computation [7,8] offers another strategy. Over-the-air FL, built on this idea, manages FL aggregation amidst interference, making it more efficient, resource-conservative, and faster than FL using orthogonal transmission. However, previous research on over-the-air FL has assumed analog modulation, in which the transmitter can freely shape the carrier waveform by choosing any real number I/Q coefficients [9,10,11,12,13]. This may not be possible for existing wireless devices, which come with digital modulation chips that may not support arbitrary modulation schemes. Moreover, following a power control approach, past work requires perfect channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT) for all devices to determine their transmission powers and counteract wireless channel effects during aggregation. In this approach, there are physical constraints on both instantaneous and average transmission power. Consequently, a device with poor channel conditions may either be unable to take part in the learning process or be required to use exceptionally high power [9,10,11,13,12]. Past work also requires perfect synchronization among the transmitters. These prerequisites lead to substantial overhead for channel estimation training and feedback before any transmission, causing increased delays and reduced spectral efficiency.

The special case of over-the-air FL using BPSK modulation is studied in [13]. While it significantly reduces implementation cost and resource requirements, one-bit quantization can result in high latency and a performance gap with the non-quantized case [14]. Furthermore, the challenges related to channel estimation and power control persist.

Most wireless systems use a constant power for blind transmission, without directly adjusting for the channel. Beyond not requiring CSIT and power control, this approach offers several advantages. First, it maintains the average energy for signal transmission regardless of how the channel varies. Additionally, it prevents the dynamic range of the transmitted signal from enlarging, making hardware implementations significantly simpler and cheaper. Lastly, approaches that adjust for the channel at the transmitter can suffer from channel estimation errors, causing the values to be multiplied by unpredictable gains when received [15]. With these considerations, [16] proposes a blind over-the-air FL strategy. However, since it relies on a particular receiver equalization, this method calls for a large number of receiver antennas, and the impact of wireless fading diminishes as the antenna count grows without bound. On the other hand, [15,17] investigate blind over-the-air FL that does not compensate for the adverse effects of fading.

In this work, we propose a joint source-channel coding scheme that incorporates novel transmission and aggregation strategies using lattice codes with adjustable quantization levels. By developing a novel coding base, we aim to enhance the resilience of over-the-air FL against noise and interference, ensuring that the desired learning outcomes are realized. In particular, this ensures effective performance in challenging channel conditions, even with a limited number of antennas at the server. Notably, our blind approach does not rely on any prior knowledge or CSIT. It is inspired by past research [18,19,20,21] showing the advantages of nested lattice coding based modulation in compute-and-forward relaying as a channel coding scheme, which enhances bit-rate throughput at relays. The key contributions are as follows.

Compute-Update Scheme: We provide an end-to-end framework for transmitting real-valued model parameters in FL, named compute-update FL— FedCPU. On the transmitter side, we develop lattice codes for quantizing the model parameters, based on normalization and dithering. On the server side, we decode a single integer combination of the transmitted quantized model parameters as a lattice point, which after processing yields a new form of aggregation. We use integer combinations because the aggregation of model parameters in FL has an additive structure. Additionally, the lattice Voronoi region over the decoded integer combination protects against the decoding error arising from interference and noise. This protection is absent in analog modulation schemes, given their continuous transmitted values [9,10,11,13,12,15,17,16]. Also, our adjustable aggregation method is a significant shift from the traditional FL practice of employing fixed, predefined weights, either equal or based on the size of local datasets. This conventional approach, recommended for ideal, error-free communication conditions in the seminal FL paper [1], has been used consistently in over-the-air FL research [9,10,1,2,11,13,12,15,17,16,14,3,4], even though over-the-air FL deals with imperfect communication plagued by interference and noise. In response, our method tailors the aggregation weights to the wide range of decoding errors unique to each integer combination in our model.

Transmitter-Receiver Architecture: To accomplish the aggregation, we propose a two-layer receiver architecture at the server side that uses both the real and imaginary parts of the signal. The first layer incorporates an equalization vector, which is optimized to minimize the decoding error. In the second layer, a normalizing factor is introduced and optimized to minimize the quantization error.

System Insights: Our experimental results highlight the efficacy of FedCPU in addressing the lack of CSIT and the presence of only a limited number of antennas at the server. Shrinking the lattice Voronoi regions reveals a balance between increased decoding error and diminished quantization error. FedCPU shows markedly superior learning accuracy compared to other over-the-air schemes, owing to its distinctive aggregation technique and finely-tuned receiver design. The learning results closely follow those expected in an ideal, error-free orthogonal transmission.
